The Lindbergh Kidnapping. In March 1932, the twenty-month-old son of aviator Charles Lindbergh was abducted from his New Jersey home. Despite a ransom payment, the child was found dead weeks later. The subsequent investigation and trial of suspect Bruno Hauptmann became the trial of the century, dominating American media and establishing forensic techniques including ladder analysis and handwriting comparison that transformed criminal investigation.

Charles Lindbergh Jr., who was twenty months old, was taken from the Lindbergh home in Hopewell, New Jersey on March 1, 1932. A ransom note demanded fifty thousand dollars. Lindbergh and intermediaries paid the ransom, but the child was never returned alive. His body was discovered in a wooded area on May 12, 1932, with evidence of blunt-force trauma.

Bruno Hauptmann was a German-born carpenter and paroled burglar. He was arrested in September 1934 after ransom money traceable to the payment was found in his possession. The trial took place from January through February 1935 and featured expert testimony on the wooden ladder used in the kidnapping. Forensic comparison of wood grain and tool marks established linkage to Hauptmann's tools and lumber.

Handwriting experts testified that Hauptmann wrote the ransom notes. Evidence of his financial desperation and prior burglaries supported motive. Hauptmann was convicted and executed by electric chair in April 1936. He maintained his innocence throughout, and lingering questions about trial conduct and evidence reliability persist even today.

The case established pathways for forensic analysis in American law and demonstrated the power of scientific testimony in high-profile trials, making it canonically the trial of the century for mid-twentieth-century Americans.
